content.text: Convection
Introduction

Why does hot air rise? Why do radiators heat entire rooms? The answer lies in convection—the transfer of heat through the movement of fluids (liquids and gases). Understanding convection explains many natural phenomena, from sea breezes to weather patterns.
Key Concept:

Convection is the transfer of thermal energy by the bulk movement of a heated fluid (liquid or gas). Warm fluid rises because it expands and becomes less dense, while cooler, denser fluid sinks to replace it, forming a convection current.
Key Concepts
What is Convection?
Convection
is the transfer of thermal energy through the movement of a fluid (liquid or gas).
Only occurs in fluids (not in solids)
Involves bulk movement of particles
Creates circulation patterns called convection currents
Driven by differences in density
How Convection Works
A fluid is heated from below (or near a heat source)
The heated fluid
expands
and becomes
less dense
The less dense fluid
rises
Cooler, denser fluid
sinks
to take its place
This creates a continuous circulation called a
convection current
Heat is carried through the fluid by this movement

content.text: Why Convection Doesn't Occur in Solids
In solids, particles are fixed in position and cannot move freely. Convection requires particles to physically move through the material, which only happens in fluids.
Convection in Liquids
Heating Water

attrs.alt: Convection currents in a pot of heated water

content.text: Water at the bottom is heated by the stove
It expands and becomes less dense
Hot water rises to the top
Cooler water from above sinks to replace it
The sinking water is heated and rises
This circulation heats the entire pot
Ocean Currents
Warm water near the equator rises and flows toward poles
Cold polar water sinks and flows toward equator
Creates global ocean circulation patterns
Distributes heat around the planet
Convection in Gases
Hot Air Balloons
Air inside the balloon is heated
Hot air expands and becomes less dense
The balloon rises because it's less dense than surrounding air
Cooling the air makes the balloon descend
Room Heating

attrs.alt: Convection currents in a room showing warm air rising and cool air sinking

content.text: Radiator heats air nearby
Hot air rises toward the ceiling
Cool air near the floor moves toward the radiator
Convection current circulates air around the room
Note: "Radiators" mainly heat by convection, despite their name!
Sea Breezes
During the day:
Land heats up faster than sea
Air over land rises
Cooler air from sea moves in to replace it
Sea breeze blows from sea to land
At night:
Land cools faster than sea
Air over sea is now warmer and rises
Cooler air from land moves out
Land breeze blows from land to sea

content.text: Factors Affecting Convection
1. Temperature Difference
Greater temperature difference = faster convection
More heating = greater density difference = stronger currents
2. Properties of the Fluid
Different fluids have different rates of expansion
Viscosity affects flow speed
Gases convect more easily than liquids
3. Distance
Convection is effective over short to medium distances
For large distances, radiation becomes more important
Common Mistake:
Students sometimes say 'heat rises'. It is not heat that rises -- it is the hot fluid that rises because it is less dense. Heat is transferred as a result of this fluid movement.
Remember:
Convection can only occur in fluids (liquids and gases) because it requires particles to physically move and circulate. It cannot happen in solids or in a vacuum.

content.text: Worked Examples
Example 1:
Explain how a hot water heating system works.
Solution:
Water is heated in a boiler (usually in the basement or utility room)
Hot water expands and becomes less dense
Hot water rises through pipes to radiators upstairs
Heat is released from radiators to rooms
Cooler, denser water sinks back down to the boiler
The cycle continues, distributing heat throughout the house
(Note: Modern systems often use pumps to assist circulation)
Example 2:
Why should a freezer compartment be at the top of a refrigerator?
Solution:
Cold air is denser than warm air
Cold air from the freezer sinks downward
This cools the main compartment below
Warmer air rises back up to the freezer to be cooled again
Natural convection circulates cold air throughout
If the freezer were at the bottom, cold air would stay at the bottom and not circulate effectively.
Example 3:
Explain how a lava lamp works.
Solution:
A light bulb heats the bottom of the lamp
Coloured wax at the bottom is heated, expands, and becomes less dense
The hot wax rises through the liquid
At the top, away from the heat source, it cools
Cooled wax becomes denser and sinks
The cycle repeats, creating the characteristic "lava" effect
Real-World Applications
Weather Systems
Thunderstorms:
Warm, moist air rises rapidly, cools, and forms clouds
Trade winds:
Global convection patterns driven by equatorial heating
Monsoons:
Seasonal convection caused by land-sea temperature differences
Geology
Mantle convection:
Hot rock rises, cool rock sinks in Earth's mantle
Plate tectonics:
Driven by convection currents in the mantle
Volcanoes:
Rising magma due to convection
Home Heating
Radiators:
Create convection currents to heat rooms
Underfloor heating:
Warm air rises from the floor
Chimney function:
Hot gases rise and exit through the chimney
Cooking
Boiling:
Convection distributes heat through the water
Convection ovens:
Fans enhance natural convection for even cooking
Deep frying:
Convection currents in oil distribute heat
Preventing Unwanted Convection
Double Glazing
Narrow gap between panes limits convection
Air can't circulate freely in the thin gap
Combined with poor conduction of trapped air
Loft Insulation
Fibrous material traps small pockets of air
Small pockets prevent convection currents forming
Air acts as insulator without being able to circulate
Cavity Wall Insulation
Foam fills the cavity between walls
Prevents convection currents in the gap
Also reduces conduction
Common Misconceptions
"Hot air rises because it wants to"
— Hot air rises because it's less dense, and buoyancy forces push it up. It's not a choice!
"Convection happens in all materials"
— Only in fluids. Solids can't have convection because particles can't move freely.
"Radiators work by radiation"
— Mostly by convection! The name is misleading. They heat air, which circulates by convection.
"Cold air falls because it's cold"
— Cold air sinks because it's denser, not because of temperature directly.
"Convection stops when heating stops"
— Convection continues until temperature differences equalise throughout the fluid.
Practice Problems
Explain why a room heater should be placed near the floor rather than near the ceiling.
Describe the convection currents that form in a beaker of water heated from below.
Explain the cause of sea breezes during the day and land breezes at night.
Explain why smoke rises from a fire.
Explain why: a) fridges have the freezer compartment at the top (in most designs) b) houses benefit from loft insulation c) hot water tanks have immersion heaters at the bottom
Explain why a convection oven with a fan cooks food faster than a conventional oven.
Describe how convection currents in Earth's mantle relate to plate tectonics.
Summary
Convection transfers heat through fluid movement
Only occurs in fluids (liquids and gases)
Heated fluid expands, becomes less dense, and rises
Cooler, denser fluid sinks to replace it
This creates a convection current (circulation pattern)
Driven by density differences caused by temperature differences
Applications: heating systems, weather, cooking, geology
Prevented by: trapping air in small pockets, narrow gaps
"Radiators" mainly work by convection, not radiation
Answer Key
Hot air rises due to reduced density.

If the heater is near the floor, the heated air rises upward and circulates through the whole room via a convection current. If it were near the ceiling, the hot air would stay at the top (since it is already less dense than the air below) and would not circulate down to warm the room effectively. (explanation with physics reasoning)
Water at the bottom is heated first.

It expands, becomes less dense, and rises. Cooler, denser water at the top sinks to take its place. This sinking water is then heated and rises in turn, creating a continuous convection current circulating around the beaker. (explanation with physics reasoning)
During the day, land heats up faster than the sea
(land has lower specific heat capacity). Air above the land warms, expands, becomes less dense, and rises. Cooler air from above the sea moves in to replace it, creating a sea breeze.
At night, land cools faster than the sea.
Air above the sea is now relatively warmer, so it rises. Cooler air from the land moves toward the sea, creating a land breeze. (explanation with physics reasoning)
The fire heats the air around it.
The hot air expands, becomes less dense than the surrounding cooler air, and rises due to buoyancy. Smoke particles are carried upward with this rising hot air. (explanation with physics reasoning)
Cold air is denser and sinks.

With the freezer at the top, cold air sinks naturally from the freezer compartment into the main section below, cooling the whole fridge by natural convection without needing a fan. (explanation with physics reasoning)
Warm air in the house rises by convection toward the roof.

Without loft insulation, this warm air loses heat rapidly through the roof by conduction. Loft insulation traps air in small pockets, preventing convection currents forming and reducing conduction through the roof. (explanation with physics reasoning)
The heater at the bottom heats the water closest to it first.

This hot water rises by convection, and cooler water sinks to replace it, creating a convection current that heats the entire tank efficiently. If the heater were at the top, only the water at the top would be heated, with no convection to distribute the heat downward. (explanation with physics reasoning)
The fan forces hot air to circulate around the food more quickly

than natural convection alone. This maintains a larger temperature difference at the food's surface and replaces the layer of cooler air that forms around the food. Energy is transferred to the food more rapidly, so it cooks faster and more evenly. (explanation with physics reasoning)
Radioactive decay in Earth's core and mantle produces heat.

Hot, less dense rock deep in the mantle rises slowly toward the surface. At the surface it cools, becomes denser, and sinks back down. These convection currents drag the tectonic plates on the surface, causing them to move. This movement drives continental drift, earthquakes, and volcanic activity at plate boundaries. (explanation with physics reasoning)
